hints.title: List a complete period
hints.body: The angles increase by π3, so six increments add 2π. Write the six sine values before using any formula for a sum.
hints.pitfall: These terms are neither one arithmetic progression nor one geometric progression.
hints.pause: Express the first six terms as multiples of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mrow><mn>3</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>.

recall.reminder: Read the terms first, then decide whether the sequence is periodic or a progression.

hints.title: Sum within the block
hints.body: Make a table with one row for each position in the repeating block. Record both the term and the running sum up to that position; these are different quantities.
hints.recap: The block total and the partial-block totals both matter.
hints.pitfall: The period of the terms is not by itself the answer to a partial-sum condition.
hints.pause: Calculate the block total and identify the partial sums equal to the target.

recall.reminder: Periodic summands still require a check of leftover partial blocks.

hints.title: Describe all successful indices
hints.body: Record which positions in your six-term running-sum table equal the target. Express their recurring indices algebraically and compare with the listed conditions.
hints.recap: Complete blocks and the residual position together determine a partial sum.
hints.pitfall: A necessary-and-sufficient condition must include every successful position and exclude every other one.
hints.pause: Derive the index condition and verify both directions using the block total.

recall.reminder: Complete blocks and the residual position together determine a partial sum.

solution:
Put c=32. The summands for k=1, …, 6 are c, c, 0, −c, −c, 0, and this block repeats because sine has period 2π. Its total is zero.

The running sums within a block are c,2c,2c,c,0,0. Therefore the required sum equals c exactly when n leaves remainder 1 or 4 on division by 6. These are precisely the positive integers n=1, 4, 7, 10, …, or n≡1(mod3).

Every such n works because complete six-term blocks contribute zero; every other remainder gives 0 or 2c instead. This proves both directions.

Answer D: n is 1 more than a multiple of 3.
knowledgePattern: Track partial sums across a six-term trigonometric cycle
